traditional.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

ait.text: And I in turn tell you: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

note.text: The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation to keep the sense a first-century hearer would have caught.

traditional.text: Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.

ait.text: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that people will praise them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

note.text: The Greek word originally meant a stage actor, but in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it already meant a godless or insincere person, and elsewhere this translation renders it 'hypocrites'. In this chapter the passage is about religion staged for an audience, with trumpets, street corners and being seen. The theatrical sense is therefore live, and 'performers' is used in verses 2, 5 and 16.

traditional.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

ait.text: The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

note.text: The Greek word means 'single' or 'sound', and most translations keep the physical image with 'healthy'. The saying sits between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, however, and the contrasting 'evil eye' was a Jewish idiom for stinginess. The saying is therefore taken to be about generosity. The physical picture of a sound eye is lost in this rendering.

traditional.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

ait.text: and saying, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

note.text: 'Repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the Hebrew prophets' call to 'return' to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life. The related noun in verses 8 and 11 is rendered 'turning back'.

traditional.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

ait.text: In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God.

note.text: Greek logos means word, speech, message or reason. Nearly all translations render it 'Word', and most scholars see John's main background in the Hebrew Bible: God creating by speaking in Genesis 1, 'the word of the Lord', and the figure of Wisdom, which 'Word' reflects and 'Logos' does not. Greek-speaking readers would also have heard the philosophical sense of logos as the reason that orders the world. The Greek term is kept here as a title because 'the Word' is now commonly taken to mean the Bible, which is not what John means.
